title: /analyze runs whole-video YOLO analysis synchronously on the backend event loop, which can stall the service for every community
description: The analyze handler is declared async def, but it calls get_engine().analyze_video(...), then insert_event for each event and dispatch_alerts, all synchronously and without asyncio.to_thread or an executor. analyze_video decodes every frame of the upload and runs YOLO (and pose when people are detected) on every sample_every-th frame, with no frame, duration or time cap. dispatch_alerts sleeps 0.5 s per event and can wait up to 5 s per MQTT publish and 10 s per Telegram request. The shipped backend image starts uvicorn with a single worker. Source therefore indicates that while one resident's upload is analysed, the single event loop cannot advance other users' async work: WebSocket live frames, /ingest, the /analyze session check and every middleware pass, which all route through the asyncio loop. Analysis time grows with the frame count of an upload of up to 200 MB, which the uploader controls. The length and breadth of the stall were not observed because no target code could be executed in this run.
claimed_root_cause: CPU-bound and network-bound blocking work (whole-video decode and YOLO inference, per-event DB inserts, MQTT and Telegram dispatch with sleeps) runs inline in an async FastAPI handler on the only event loop, with no worker offload, concurrency limit or frame/time budget.

trace.description: POST /analyze handler declared async def, so its body runs on the event loop thread; any authenticated resident or community_admin can call it.
get_engine().analyze_video(tmp_path, EVIDENCE_DIR, source_label=label) is called synchronously, with no asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.
while True: cap.read() iterates over every decoded frame with no frame-count or time cap.
self.detector.detect(frame) runs YOLO inference for each sampled frame on the calling thread, which is the event loop thread.

evidence.description: ws_live offloads per-frame inference with asyncio.to_thread, showing the intended pattern that /analyze does not follow.
insert_event (synchronous psycopg2 work) runs on the event loop for every detected event.
dispatch_alerts calls time.sleep(0.5) per event, on the event loop when called from analyze at line 609.
MQTTActuator._send waits up to 5 s per siren/LED command (wait_for_publish(timeout=5)); with the tracked config.yaml, actuator.type is mqtt.
The Telegram sendPhoto request in dispatch_alerts can block for up to 10 s when Telegram credentials are configured.
uvicorn starts without --workers, so one process and one event loop serve every community; docker-compose.yml does not override the command.
MAX_UPLOAD_MB bounds bytes only; no frame, duration or time limit exists on the analysis path.
Inference is skipped only for frames that are not multiples of sample_every (3 in config.yaml), so inference count scales linearly with frame count.

blockers: The claimed effect is a runtime event-loop stall; no target code could be executed in this run (no OS-enforced sandbox), so the stall was not observed and its duration for a given upload is unmeasured.
The number of uvicorn worker processes actually running in the deployment is a deployment fact; source shows a single worker in backend/Dockerfile but an operator could run a different command.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox with CPU, memory and wall-clock limits and no external network, run the backend against a disposable PostgreSQL with one dummy resident, the shipped single-worker uvicorn command, actuator.type set to log and Telegram unset. Replace GuardianEngine.analyze_video with a stub that calls time.sleep(10) and returns an empty list (or use a 60-second synthetic MP4 with the real models). Start one POST /analyze as the dummy resident with a small MP4, and 1 s later send POST /ingest with a dummy edge token (or open /ws/live as a second dummy resident and send one JPEG). Record the second request's latency; stop once it is shown to wait for the analysis to finish.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks the command the backend container actually runs (docker inspect of the container's Cmd/Args) to confirm whether uvicorn uses a single worker.

title: Upload and ingest size limits rely only on the declared Content-Length, so chunked bodies are received in full before any limit applies
description: limitar_subidas is documented as rejecting oversized /analyze uploads before they are received, but upload_too_big reads only the Content-Length header and treats a missing header as '0'. A request sent with Transfer-Encoding: chunked carries no Content-Length and passes. The analyze handler takes an UploadFile parameter, so FastAPI parses the whole multipart body, spooling the file part to a temporary file, before the handler's own 200 MB counter runs; that counter only limits the second copy into UPLOAD_DIR. The repository Caddyfile sets no request body limit, and backend port 8000 is also published directly. An authenticated resident can therefore stream an arbitrarily large body into the container's temporary storage on the shared host disk for as long as the request lasts. /ingest has the same pattern for edge-device token holders: its 100 kB check reads only Content-Length and request.json() buffers the full body in memory. Whether the installed Starlette/python-multipart versions impose their own file-part limit, and what disk backs the spool, are not visible in source.
claimed_root_cause: Request body size is enforced from a client-declared header instead of counting bytes actually received during parsing, and neither the ASGI layer nor the repository proxy configuration applies a streaming body limit.

trace.description: HTTP middleware for POST /analyze: session check, then size check.
upload_too_big(request) is the only pre-receipt size control.
int(request.headers.get('content-length', '0')): a chunked request without Content-Length is treated as 0 bytes.
call_next forwards the request; FastAPI parses the full multipart form to build the UploadFile before invoking the handler.
The video: UploadFile parameter has already been spooled in full by the framework, with no application size limit, before the handler body runs.

evidence.description: The docstring states the intent to reject huge uploads before receiving them, using Content-Length.
The handler's byte counter applies only while copying out of the already-parsed UploadFile.
/ingest checks size through the Content-Length header only.
request.json() reads the entire /ingest body into memory.
reverse_proxy has no request_body max_size.
Backend port 8000 is published directly, bypassing the proxy.
fastapi>=0.110.0 is unpinned (as is python-multipart at line 10), so the installed multipart spooling behaviour depends on the build.

blockers: Starlette and python-multipart versions in the built image are unpinned; whether they impose any size limit on multipart file parts, and where they spool them, must be confirmed for the built image without executing it here.
Whether Caddy and any host or CDN in front of it forward chunked request bodies to the backend without a bound is a deployment fact.
The location of the container's temporary directory, its free space, and whether that filesystem is shared with ./events and PostgreSQL are deployment facts.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox with no external network, CPU/memory/time limits, TMPDIR on a 64 MB size-limited tmpfs and MAX_UPLOAD_MB=1, run the backend against a disposable PostgreSQL with a dummy resident session. POST /analyze with Transfer-Encoding: chunked and a 5 MB multipart file part; observe that limitar_subidas does not return 413 and that the spool file in TMPDIR grows past 1 MB before the handler returns its own 413. Repeat for /ingest with a dummy edge token and a 1 MB chunked JSON body, observing process RSS. Stop at the first exceedance.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner confirms whether any request body limit exists in front of the backend (none is set in the repository Caddyfile), whether port 8000 is reachable from the Internet, and the free space and sharing of the filesystem backing the container's /tmp.

title: One resident can open unlimited /ws/live sessions and starve other tenants' live detection on the shared inference lock and default thread pool
description: /ws/live accepts any number of concurrent connections per user and per camera, and processes every binary frame the client sends; the only pacing (one frame in flight) is in the dashboard JavaScript, which a scripted client need not follow. Each frame is handed to asyncio.to_thread, which uses the event loop's default executor (bounded by min(32, CPU count + 4) threads), and then waits on the single process-wide engine.infer_lock. Because each connection keeps one to_thread call in flight, a resident who opens enough connections and sends small valid JPEGs back to back can keep most default-executor threads busy waiting on infer_lock. Other residents' live sessions in any community then get a fraction of inference throughput, and other asyncio.to_thread work queues behind it: /ingest token lookups and inserts, WebSocket authentication and camera resolution, and the /analyze session check. Synchronous def routes run in anyio's separate thread pool and are not affected by the default-executor queue. The degree of starvation is a runtime property that was not observed.
claimed_root_cause: The server has no per-user or per-camera limit on concurrent live sessions or frame rate and no fair scheduling for the shared inference lock; pacing is delegated to the browser client.

trace.description: Authenticated WebSocket handler; nothing counts or limits concurrent connections per user or camera.
resolve_camera checks only that the camera is the user's own active private camera; it keeps no session accounting.
receive_bytes loop with no rate, count or application-level size limit.
Each frame is submitted with asyncio.to_thread to the shared default executor.
cv2.imdecode decodes client bytes in the worker thread before the lock.
with eng.infer_lock: detect and pose run under one process-wide lock shared by every user and community.

evidence.description: A single threading.Lock (no fairness guarantee) guards the shared YOLO models for all clients.
The comment states one frame is sent and the reply awaited so the model never saturates; this pacing exists only in the client.
resolve_camera's query matches an own, active, private camera and records nothing about open connections.
/ingest's edge token lookup uses asyncio.to_thread, sharing the same default executor.
The limitar_subidas session lookup for /analyze uses asyncio.to_thread, sharing the same default executor.
A single uvicorn process hosts every tenant's live sessions.
The repository reverse_proxy block sets no limit on concurrent WebSocket connections per client.

blockers: The default executor size depends on the deployed host's CPU count, and per-frame inference latency depends on host CPU and torch threading; neither is visible in source, and nothing could be executed in this run.
How unevenly threading.Lock acquisitions are distributed under contention, and therefore how much a victim session's throughput falls, is runtime behaviour that was not observed.

Whether any layer in front of the backend (host firewall, CDN, or a different proxy configuration) limits concurrent WebSocket connections per client or user is a deployment fact; the repository Caddyfile sets none and port 8000 is published directly.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox with CPU, memory and wall-clock limits and no external network, run the backend against a disposable PostgreSQL with two dummy residents in two dummy communities, replacing detector.detect with a stub that sleeps 50 ms under infer_lock. Open one victim /ws/live connection that sends one small JPEG per reply, then N = 4, 8 and 16 attacker connections from the other dummy resident that send 1 KB valid JPEGs back to back. Record victim frames per second and the latency of one concurrent POST /ingest with a dummy edge token at each N. Stop once victim throughput clearly falls with N.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks the backend host's CPU count, whether any proxy or firewall in front of intivision.online or port 8000 limits concurrent WebSocket connections per client IP or user, and the expected number of simultaneous live users.

title: Evidence images are written to the shared evidence directory without per-user quota or retention, so one resident may exhaust storage for all communities
description: Every MEDIO/ALTO event writes a full-resolution JPEG of the decoded frame into the shared events/ directory, bind-mounted from host ./events. /analyze produces up to one image per 5 s of video time with no frame or duration cap, and /ws/live up to one per 5 s per session with unlimited sessions. No application code deletes evidence files, caps per-user totals, or enforces the per-plan quota the schema defines (plans.storage_gb and v_user_storage.quota_bytes are never referenced from Python). Image size follows the decoded frame resolution, which the uploader controls, and a compact long video of a static high-resolution scene with a person loitering could turn one upload of at most 200 MB into many large persistent evidence files. If the shared disk fills, other tenants' evidence writes fail silently (cv2.imwrite's return value is ignored while the event is still recorded), and anything else on that filesystem is affected. The bytes written per upload and the disk layout were not observed.
claimed_root_cause: Persisted evidence is not accounted per principal and has no quota, size cap or retention, and the write paths never enforce the schema-level quota (plans.storage_gb / v_user_storage).

trace.description: An authenticated resident uploads a video (live sessions reach the same kind of write at engine.py:153).
Every MEDIO/ALTO result at least event_cooldown_s (5 s) of video time after the previous one becomes an event, for the whole video.
cv2.imwrite writes a full-resolution JPEG of the frame into the shared evidence directory, where nothing ever deletes it.

evidence.description: Live sessions persist one evidence image per event per session into the same directory.
Live sessions are created with the shared EVIDENCE_DIR.
plans.storage_gb defines a per-plan storage quota.
The v_user_storage quota view exists, but no Python code references it or plans.storage_gb.
The evidence directory is a host bind mount shared by all communities.
MAX_UPLOAD_MB caps input bytes only, not decoded output volume.

blockers: The bytes each event can write (decoded-resolution limits of the bundled FFmpeg/OpenCV and the JPEG size of attacker-chosen frames) can only be learned by running the decoder, which was not possible in this run.
The host's disk capacity, whether ./events shares a filesystem with PostgreSQL data and Docker storage, and whether any operator cleanup job exists are deployment facts.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox with no external network, CPU/memory/time limits and a 256 MB size-limited filesystem for the events directory, run analyze_video with a stub detector and scorer that return ALTO for every sampled frame. Analyse one synthetic MP4 of at most 5 MB showing a static high-resolution scene, as a dummy resident through the local backend or directly via GuardianEngine. Measure total bytes written to events/ against the input size, and stop at the quota.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks the disk capacity and filesystem layout behind ./events, whether PostgreSQL data shares that filesystem, and whether any retention or cleanup job runs.
